subject: RFP: Topology Partitioning & Threat Reduction Questionnaire
messages:
From: Carlos Vega <carlos.vega@atlasbank.com>
To: diego_fernandez@redwood.ai
Cc: Atlas Bank Security <security@atlasbank.com>
Date: Wed, 10 Apr 2029 08:22:00 -0700
Subject: Atlas RFP: Topology partitioning and attack surface questionnaire

Diego,

Thanks for taking our questionnaire — attached is Atlas Bank's standard topology partitioning worksheet and a short list of follow-ups we need answered before our security committee will greenlight vendor evaluation. High level asks:

- A network diagram showing tenant demarcation and control-plane/data-plane separation for the hosted service.
- Clear description of egress controls for tenant workloads (bastion, peering, firewall rules).
- Threat scenarios that would allow cross-tenant data access and mitigation rationale.
- Evidence that shows operator access is scoped and auditable (logs/evidence).

We'd appreciate a concise narrative (and any diagram attachments) we can include in the committee packet. Our deadline for the packet is Friday EOD (2029-04-12).

Attached: Atlas_topology_workbook.xlsx (questionnaire)

Thanks,
Carlos Vega
Senior Information Security Manager
Atlas Bank

From: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Vega <carlos.vega@atlasbank.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 10 Apr 2029 11:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Atlas RFP: Topology partitioning and attack surface questionnaire

Carlos —

Appreciate the clear asks. We're on it; putting a short packet together and will include a deployment diagram and a short threat-summary tailored to the questions you highlighted. Preliminary notes below and we'll attach formal artifacts by Friday: 

1) High-level architecture (summary):
   - Control plane (multi-tenant, Redwood-managed) is isolated in a separate VPC with strict management-plane peering. Control-plane APIs authenticate operator actions via mutual-TLS and an internal RBAC service.
   - Data plane (customer inference workloads) runs in per-tenant compute pools. For our hosted offering, each tenant’s inference containers are placed into logical tenant subnets on isolated host pools; no tenant VM/container shares the same dedicated PCI-VM with another tenant at the same time.

2) Egress & network controls:
   - Tenant egress is policy-enforced via a sidecar-managed egress proxy. By default external egress is blocked; customers can request explicit outbound allowlists.
   - We offer private connectivity (VPC peering or PrivateLink) for regulated customers; those paths bypass public internet egress and are subject to network ACLs and Flow Logs.

3) Cross-tenant threat scenarios & mitigations (short):
   - KV cache leakage: KV caches are namespaced per-tenant with encryption keys derived and scoped per tenant; caches are not stored on shared filesystem beyond lifecycle of inference worker.
   - Sidecar compromise: sidecars are hardened, run with minimal privileges, and constrained by network namespaces; we enforce strict process-level auditing and immutable sidecar images.
   - Control-plane impersonation: mutual-TLS + signed operator audit events + KMS-backed key rotation limits replay or reuse.

4) Operator access & auditing:
   - All operator actions require 2FA, are logged to an append-only telemetry service, and tied to individual SSO identities. We retain logs for 13 months by default and can extend for enterprise contracts.

We'll attach: redwood_topology_v1.drawio (diagram), isolation_evidence_manifest.pdf (evidence list), and a 2-page threat-summary. Is there a preferred format for the committee packet (single PDF vs separate attachments)?

Thanks — I'll loop Marissa for architecture-level attachments and Ben for logs/evidence.

— Diego
Diego Fernandez
Director, Solutions Architecture
Redwood Inference

From: Carlos Vega <carlos.vega@atlasbank.com>
To: diego_fernandez@redwood.ai
Cc: Atlas Bank Security <security@atlasbank.com>
Date: Thu, 11 Apr 2029 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Atlas RFP: Topology partitioning and attack surface questionnaire

Diego —

Thanks, that summary is useful. Two quick clarifications before you prepare the packet: 

- When you say "logical tenant subnets on isolated host pools", do you provide hardware-level affinity options (i.e., dedicated hosts) or is isolation strictly software-enforced on shared hosts? We need both options and clear SLA differences.
- For KV cache namespacing and encryption: can you confirm whether caching keys are derived per-tenant using a KMS key per customer (customer-managed KMS for Private offering), or are keys managed centrally by Redwood?

Also: our compliance team is specifically asking for:
  * A small attack tree describing a plausible lateral movement path from a compromised tenant container to control-plane credentials.
  * An example of a red-team test we could request as part of the vendor assessment (low-impact, scoped).

If you can provide concise answers to those bullets alongside the diagram, that should be sufficient for our committee packet.

Carlos

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Vega <carlos.vega@atlasbank.com>
Cc: diego_fernandez@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 12 Apr 2029 16:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Atlas RFP: Topology partitioning and attack surface questionnaire

Carlos —

Attaching the packet for your committee (short package + appendices). Answers below and attached artifacts: redwood_topology_v1.drawio, isolation_evidence_manifest.pdf, attack_tree_sample.txt (attack tree summary), redteam_scoping_example.md. (Attachments have been uploaded to the secure drive link included at the top of this message.)

Direct answers to your clarifications: 

- Dedicated hosts vs software isolation: 
  * We offer three deployment modes: Hosted (software-enforced multi-tenant isolation on shared hosts), Dedicated Capacity (tenant-dedicated GPU host pools), and Private (customer-managed VPC / on-prem). Dedicated Capacity provides single-tenant host affinity and stronger SLA guarantees (throughput and isolation). Pricing and provisioning lead times differ; we included a matrix in Appendix A.

- KV cache key management: 
  * For Hosted customers, cache encryption keys are generated and managed by Redwood KMS (isolated per-tenant key material).
  * For Dedicated and Private customers we support customer-managed keys (CMK) via KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS) so that key material can be customer-owned. This is in the manifest (see isolation_evidence_manifest.pdf).

- Attack tree (summary): 
  * Initial access: compromised third-party model artifact or malicious prompt payload uploads.
  * Local privilege escalation: exploit in sidecar or runtime leading to container breakout.
  * Lateral movement: attempt to access shared KV or metadata endpoints; mitigations include namespace enforcement and strict egress rules.
  * Control-plane access: try to reuse leaked operator tokens; mitigations include short-lived certs, mutual-TLS, and anomaly detection.

- Red-team test (scoped example): 
  * Objective: validate tenant isolation without disrupting production.
  * Scope: staging environment with identical topology, synthetic payloads only, simulated cache poisoning attempt, and monitoring validation.
  * Success criteria: exploit attempts fail to access cross-tenant resources; telemetry and alerts trigger within expected thresholds.

We have also attached audit log samples and a redacted KMS usage report to demonstrate operator scoping and rotation. If the committee wants a brief walkthrough, Diego and I can join for a 30-minute session next week.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Security Architect (Solutions)
Redwood Inference
